claim: On September 26, 2025 AWS raised the gp3 maximums to 64 TiB, 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s per volume. Before that, the limits were 16 TiB, 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s.
question: When did the gp3 volume maximums change, and what were the old and new size, IOPS and throughput limits?

evidence.quote: | [gp3 volume updates](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/general-purpose.html#gp3-ebs-volume-type) | You can now provision General Purpose SSD (gp3) volumes with sizes up to 64 TiB, IOPS up to 80,000, and throughput up to 2,000 MiB/s. | September 26, 2025 |

With this update, gp3 volumes can scale up to 64 TiB in size (4X the previous 16 TiB limit), up to 80,000 IOPS (5X the previous 16,000 IOPS limit), and up to 2,000 MiB/s throughput (2X the previous 1,000 MiB/s limit).

claim: A gp3 volume can be provisioned with up to 80,000 IOPS, at a ratio of 500 IOPS per GiB, so the maximum needs a volume of 160 GiB or larger. Before September 26, 2025 the maximum was 16,000 IOPS.
question: What is the maximum IOPS of one gp3 volume, and what volume size does it need?

values.spoken: one hundred sixty gibibytes or larger

qualifiers.condition: additional IOPS above the 3,000 IOPS baseline cost extra; outside AWS Outposts

evidence.quote: You can provision additional IOPS (up to a maximum of 80,000) for an additional cost at a ratio of 500 IOPS per GiB of volume size. Maximum IOPS can be provisioned for volumes 160 GiB or larger (500 IOPS per GiB × 160 GiB = 80,000 IOPS).

With this update, gp3 volumes can scale up to 64 TiB in size (4X the previous 16 TiB limit), up to 80,000 IOPS (5X the previous 16,000 IOPS limit), and up to 2,000 MiB/s throughput (2X the previous 1,000 MiB/s limit).

claim: A gp3 volume can be provisioned with up to 2,000 MiB/s of throughput, at a ratio of 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS. Before September 26, 2025 the maximum was 1,000 MiB/s.
question: What is the maximum throughput of one gp3 volume?

values.spoken: a quarter mebibyte per second per provisioned IOPS

qualifiers.condition: throughput above the 125 MiB/s baseline costs extra; outside AWS Outposts

evidence.quote: You can provision additional throughput (up to a maximum of 2,000 MiB/s) for an additional cost at a ratio of 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS.

With this update, gp3 volumes can scale up to 64 TiB in size (4X the previous 16 TiB limit), up to 80,000 IOPS (5X the previous 16,000 IOPS limit), and up to 2,000 MiB/s throughput (2X the previous 1,000 MiB/s limit).

claim: A gp3 volume can range in size from 1 GiB to 64 TiB. Before September 26, 2025 the maximum size was 16 TiB.
question: What is the size range of a gp3 volume?

evidence.quote: A gp3 volume can range in size from 1 GiB to 64 TiB.

With this update, gp3 volumes can scale up to 64 TiB in size (4X the previous 16 TiB limit), up to 80,000 IOPS (5X the previous 16,000 IOPS limit), and up to 2,000 MiB/s throughput (2X the previous 1,000 MiB/s limit).

claim: As of April 30, 2025, every io2 volume, new or previously created, is an io2 Block Express volume.
question: Since when is every io2 volume an io2 Block Express volume?

evidence.quote: As of **April 30, 2025**, all new and previously created `io2` volumes are `io2` Block Express volumes.

note: FRESHNESS dated the change 2023-11-21 (Nitro) and 2025-07-22 (Regions); the provisioned-iops page gives April 30, 2025 for all io2 volumes. No page states the old io2 limits verbatim, so no 'was'. The 2023-11-21 What's New page is blocked by robots.txt.

claim: On July 22, 2025 io2 volumes became available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.
question: When did io2 volumes become available in all commercial Regions?

evidence.quote: | [`io2` Region expansion](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/provisioned-iops.html#io2-block-express) | Provisioned IOPS SSD (`io2`) volumes are now available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. | July 22, 2025 |

claim: Attached to Nitro-based instances, io2 Block Express volumes are designed for an average latency under 500 microseconds for 16 KiB I/O, and they cut the frequency of I/Os over 800 microseconds by more than 10 times compared with General Purpose volumes.
question: What average latency is io2 Block Express designed for, and how does its outlier latency compare with gp3?

qualifiers.condition: attached to Nitro-based instances; 16 KiB I/O operations

evidence.quote: When attached to [ Nitro-based instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/instancetypes/ec2-nitro-instances.html), `io2` Block Express volumes are designed to deliver an average latency of under 500 microseconds for 16KiB I/O operations. `io2` Block Express volumes also deliver better outlier latency compared to General Purpose volumes, reducing the frequency of I/Os exceeding 800 microseconds by over 10 times.

| [Latency guidance updates for io2 volumes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/provisioned-iops.html#io2-block-express) | `io2` Block Express volumes are designed to deliver an average latency of under 500 microseconds for 16KiB I/O operations. `io2` Block Express volumes also deliver better outlier latency compared to General Purpose volumes, reducing the frequency of I/Os exceeding 800 microseconds by over 10 times. | September 26, 2025 |

note: Latency guidance updated in the history on September 26, 2025; the earlier wording is not stated verbatim.

claim: On January 15, 2026 Elastic Volumes changed: you can start a new modification as soon as the previous one completes, up to four times within a 24-hour period.
question: What changed for Elastic Volumes modification frequency in January 2026?

values.display: up to four times within a 24-hour period

evidence.quote: | [Elastic Volumes modification update](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-modify-volume.html) |  You can now initiate a new Elastic Volumes modification as soon as the previous one completes, up to four times within a 24-hour period.  | January 15, 2026 |
With this update, you can start a new modification immediately after the previous one completes, as long as you have initiated fewer than four modifications in the past 24 hours.

note: FRESHNESS says the old rule was a 6-hour wait between modifications; neither the history row nor the announcement states the old value, so it is not recorded.

claim: You can modify one EBS volume up to four times within a rolling 24-hour period, provided the volume is in-use or available and every earlier modification of it is completed.
question: How often can you modify one EBS volume with Elastic Volumes?

values.display: up to four times within a rolling 24-hour period
values.spoken: up to four times in any twenty-four hours

qualifiers.condition: the previous modification must be completed first

evidence.quote: You can modify a volume up to four times within a rolling 24-hour period, as long as the volume is in the `in-use` or `available` state, and all previous modifications for that volume are `completed`.

claim: On November 20, 2025 Recycle Bin started to protect EBS volumes against accidental deletion; before, it covered snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs.
question: Since when can Recycle Bin recover deleted EBS volumes, and what did it cover before?

evidence.quote: | [Recycle Bin for EBS volumes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/recycle-bin.html) | Recycle Bin enables you to protect Amazon EBS volumes against accidental deletions. | November 20, 2025 |
Recycle Bin for Amazon EBS, which helps you recover accidentally deleted snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs, now supports EBS Volumes.

claim: Recycle Bin lets you restore accidentally deleted EBS volumes, EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs; deleted resources stay in the Recycle Bin for a retention period you set before they are permanently deleted.
question: Which deleted resources can Recycle Bin restore?

values.display: EBS volumes, EBS snapshots, and EBS-backed AMIs
for a time period that you specify

qualifiers.condition: a retention rule must match the resource

evidence.quote: Recycle Bin is a data recovery feature that enables you to restore accidentally deleted EBS volumes, EBS snapshots, and EBS-backed AMIs. When using Recycle Bin, if your resources are deleted, they are retained in the Recycle Bin for a time period that you specify before being permanently deleted.

claim: Recycle Bin and its retention rules have no additional charge, but volumes kept in the Recycle Bin are billed at the same rate as regular volumes.
question: What do you pay for deleted EBS volumes kept in the Recycle Bin?

values.display: billed at the same price as EBS Volumes

evidence.quote: There are no additional charges for using Recycle Bin and retention rules.
EBS Volumes in Recycle Bin are billed at the same price as EBS Volumes, read more on the pricing page.

claim: On October 14, 2025 EBS added volume copy: an instant, point-in-time copy of a volume within the same Availability Zone.
question: When did EBS add the ability to copy a volume directly?

evidence.quote: | [Copy an EBS volume](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-copying-volume.html) | You can create an instant, point-in-time copy of an Amazon EBS volume within the same Availability Zone.  | October 14, 2025 |

claim: A volume copy is a crash-consistent, point-in-time copy of the source volume, and it must be created in the same Availability Zone as the source volume.
question: Where can you create a copy of an EBS volume, and what kind of copy is it?

values.display: same Availability Zone as the source volume

evidence.quote: A volume copy is a crash-consistent, point-in-time copy of the source volume.
The volume copy must be created in the same Availability Zone as the source volume.

claim: A volume copy is created immediately and can be accessed at once, without waiting for the data to be copied from the source volume; the copy operation does not affect the performance of the source volume.
question: How fast can you use an EBS volume copy, and does copying slow the source volume?

qualifiers.condition: during initialization the copy gets baseline performance

evidence.quote: Volume copies are created immediately and can be attached to an Amazon EC2 instance once it reaches the `available` state.

Copy operations don't affect the performance of the source volume. You can continue using the source volume normally during the copy process. Copied volumes can be accessed instantly without waiting for the data to be copied from the source volume.

claim: Copying a volume has a copy-operation charge based on the size of the data blocks written to the source volume when the copy is created; the new volume is then charged like any other EBS volume.
question: What do you pay for when you copy an EBS volume?

values.display: size of the data blocks written to the source volume

evidence.quote: When you create a copy of a source volume, you are charged for the copy operation. The copy operation charge is based on the size of the data blocks written to the source volume at the time of copy creation. The newly created volume is charged the same way as any other Amazon EBS volume.

claim: Posted on Sep 9, 2026: EBS Volume Clones added copying volumes across AWS accounts, with re-encryption under an AWS KMS key of the target account.
question: When could EBS volumes first be copied across accounts?

values.display: copying EBS volumes across AWS accounts

qualifiers.condition: GA after the 2026-07-15 cutoff: not examinable yet

evidence.quote: Posted on: Sep 9, 2026
evidence.heading: Amazon EBS Volume Clones now supports copying volumes across accounts

evidence.quote: Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Volume Clones now supports copying EBS volumes across AWS accounts with re-encryption. You can copy EBS volumes to any AWS account, re-encrypting with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key in the target account.

note: Not examinable yet (GA after 2026-07-15, RULINGS rule 7). The volume copy page already says copies can be made from volumes shared through AWS RAM.
